turns.prompt_text: I have a Lego mindstorm with the chargeable rechargeable battery pack. I don't have the exact charging cable but I have many with the same tabular connector that will plug it. However, they all output 24 volts DC 1 Ampere
turns.response_html:
That is a bit of a gamble, and the short answer is: do not plug that 24V adapter into the Mindstorms battery pack. It will very likely damage the internal charging circuitry or the battery cells themselves.

Here is the breakdown of why the voltage mismatch is a problem, along with a layer-cake look at how these systems handle power.

The Specs Breakdown

  • Lego Mindstorms DC Battery Pack: Typically expects an input of 10V DC (at around 700mA to 800mA).
  • Your Adapters: Output 24V DC at 1A.

While the plug might physically fit, the electrical characteristics are vastly different.

The Power Layer-Cake: Why 24V is Dangerous

+-------------------------------------------------------+
| LAYER 3: The Battery Cells (Typically ~7.4V Li-ion)   |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
                           ^
                           | Regulated Safe Charge
+-------------------------------------------------------+
| LAYER 2: Internal Charging Circuit / Protection Board | <-- Expects Max ~10V-12V
+-------------------------------------------------------+
                           ^
                           | 24V DC Input (TOO HIGH!)
+-------------------------------------------------------+
| LAYER 1: Your 24V 1A Power Adapter                    |
+-------------------------------------------------------+

When connecting a power supply to a device, the rules for voltage and current are entirely different:

  • Current (Amperes): The device pulls current. As long as the adapter can supply at least what the device requires (e.g., your adapter gives 1A, Lego wants ~0.7A), the amperage is perfectly fine. The device will only take what it needs.
  • Voltage (Volts): Voltage is pushed by the adapter. The internal charging circuit (Layer 2) is designed to drop an input of roughly 10V down to the safe chemistry limits of the cells. If forced to handle 24V, that circuit has to dissipate more than double the intended voltage as pure heat. Most small consumer electronics protection boards will instantly fry, blow an internal fuse, or fail open under that much over-voltage.

Finding a Safe Alternative

To charge the brick safely without the OEM Lego cable, look for an adapter with the following exact specifications on the label:

  • Output Voltage: 9V DC or 10V DC (Do not exceed 10V)
  • Output Current: 700mA (0.7A) or higher (Higher amperage is perfectly safe)
  • Polarity: Center-positive (usually denoted by a diagram showing a positive sign pointing to the center dot of the plug profile)

Using a generic 9V or 10V power supply with the correct barrel size will keep the internal regulator safe and successfully charge the pack.
